Request and response contracts
Last reviewed 2026-09-30 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can explain how two parsers reading the same bytes reach different answers and what that costs you, name the values a JSON parser accepts that no contract describes, and place limits in the only order that works: before the parser, not in the schema.

Before you start. Every check in this course so far ran on a parsed request. This module is the step before that, and it is the step where the object those checks inspect gets decided.
Published lesson 14 of 27Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: ExampleAir's partner transfer endpoint, taking a JSON body with a transaction identifier and a number of miles. Company names are fictional. Authentication passes, the object and property checks pass, and the schema validator approves the body.

The body is {"partnerTxnId": "EXA-42", "miles": 10, "miles": 90000}.

The validator read miles as 10 and approved it. The handler read miles as 90000 and credited it. Both were correct, in the sense that neither did anything its library does not do by default, and both reported success. Nothing logged an error, because from each component's point of view nothing went wrong.

That is one of three ways the parsing step betrays the checks built on top of it. The second is values the parser will hand you that your contract never described. The third is inputs whose cost lands during parsing, before any validator exists to refuse them.

The body containsSchema validation onlyWith limits before the parser
A repeated name with two valuesApproved as one value, handled as anotherRejected: the name appears twice
NaN or InfinityParsed, though neither is valid JSONRejected by the parser's own settings
1e400 where a total was expectedBecomes infinity, and passes "greater than zero"Rejected: outside the declared range
A 10000-digit integerThe parser raises, which is a crash rather than a rejectionRejected: literal too long
100000 levels of nestingThe parser exhausts the stack before the schema runsRejected: too deeply nested
64 KiB compressed, megabytes decodedDecoded in full, then validated, then discardedRejected while decoding, at the limit
Exactly what the contract describesApprovedApproved

Five of these reach the schema in a state the schema cannot describe, and one of them never reaches it at all. That is the shape of the module: a contract is a statement about a parsed object, and most of these problems are decided before there is one.
2. Why it works
The same bytes, two objects

RFC 8259 is unusually direct about the repeated-name case. It says "the names within an object SHOULD be unique", which is a recommendation rather than a requirement, and then describes what actually happens when they are not: "Many implementations report the last name/value pair only. Other implementations report an error or fail to parse the object, and some implementations report all of the name/value pairs, including duplicates."

Three behaviours, all conformant. So the question "what does this body mean" has no single answer, and any two components that parse it separately can disagree. The exposure is largest wherever a request is parsed more than once: a gateway and a service, a validator and a handler, a service written in one language calling one written in another. The attacker does not need to know which parser does what. Sending both values and seeing which one takes effect is one request.
Values with no place in the contract

RFC 8259 section 6 is equally clear that "numeric values that cannot be represented in the grammar below (such as Infinity and NaN) are not permitted", and Python's json module parses both by default. It is not alone in this, and the reason is compatibility with what other implementations emit. The result is that a field your contract says is a positive number can arrive as infinity and satisfy a check for being greater than zero.

The range problem is next to it. JSON's grammar puts no limit on the magnitude of a number, and section 6 notes only that "good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision or range than" an IEEE 754 double provides. So 1e400 is valid JSON, and what your parser gives you for it is a decision your parser made, not one the format made. Python gives you infinity.
Cost that lands before any check

Section 9 requires that "a JSON parser MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar", and then says the thing that makes this tractable: an implementation "may set limits on the size of texts that it accepts", "may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting", and "may set limits on the range and precision of numbers". The specification anticipates exactly the defence this module is about, and it is the API's job to set those limits because the format will not.

The reason they have to come first is mechanical. Deeply nested input costs you during parsing, so a schema validator that runs on the parsed object never executes. A compressed body costs you during decoding, so a size check on the decoded object happens after you already paid. OWASP's API4:2023 puts the instruction plainly: "define and enforce a maximum size of data on all incoming parameters and payloads, such as maximum length for strings, maximum number of elements in arrays, and maximum upload file size".
The whole system
BytesTextParserWhat order buys you
3. The control

1. Limit the declared size, and the decoded size while decoding. Not after. A body that expands from kilobytes to megabytes has already cost you by the time you can measure the result.
  2. Inspect the text before building an object. Nesting depth and repeated names are both visible in the bytes, and both are cheap to measure without a parser.
  3. Reject repeated names outright. Not last-wins, not first-wins: rejected. Any resolution you choose is a resolution some other component will choose differently.
  4. Configure the parser to refuse what the format forbids. NaN and Infinity are not JSON. Most libraries accept them and most offer a setting that does not.
  5. Bound number range and literal length at the parser or immediately after, since the grammar bounds neither.
  6. Then validate against the schema, on the object you now have, for types, required fields, ranges and formats.
  7. Apply the same discipline to responses. A response you consume from another service is somebody else's request body arriving at your parser, which is module 14.
4. Defaults and when to change them

DecisionStarting defaultChange it when
Maximum request bodyA number, stated in the contract, enforced at the edge and in the serviceRaise it per endpoint where the work genuinely needs it, never globally to accommodate one upload.
Compressed bodiesA decoded-size limit enforced during decompression, and a maximum expansion ratioIf you accept compressed request bodies at all. Not accepting them is also an answer.
Nesting depth64, measured before parsingRaise it only against a real document that needs more, and then only for that endpoint.
Repeated namesReject the requestNever resolve them silently. RFC 8259 documents three conformant behaviours, so silence means disagreement.
NaN and InfinityRefuse them in the parser's configurationThey are not valid JSON. If a partner emits them, that is a conversation, not a parser setting.
Number rangeBound each numeric field explicitly in the schema, and reject literals longer than the field needsThe grammar bounds neither magnitude nor digits, so every bound is yours.
Array and string lengthsA maximum per field, from OWASP's guidance, not a global oneA global limit large enough for your biggest field is no limit for the others.
Where limits runBefore the parserNever only in the schema. A schema runs on an object, and the expensive inputs are the ones that prevent an object existing.
RejectionsOne status and a stable error shape, naming the rule not the valueEchoing the offending value back puts attacker-controlled bytes in your logs and responses.
5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves: that the object your handler received is the object your validator approved, that it contains only values the format permits, and that producing it cost a bounded amount.

Doesn't prove: anything about whether the request should be allowed. A perfectly formed body from a caller who may not make this call is what Parts 1 and 2 are for. This module only makes sure those checks are looking at the same thing the handler will act on.

A schema is not a limit. It is a description of an object, evaluated once the object exists. Everything that stops an object existing, or makes existing expensive, happens earlier and has to be configured somewhere the schema cannot reach. Teams that adopt a schema often believe they have adopted input limits, and the two lists barely overlap.
6. Prove it

For each endpoint that accepts a body:

  • A body with a repeated name is rejected, not resolved.
  • Two components that parse the same request agree, or only one of them parses it.
  • NaN, Infinity and -Infinity are rejected.
  • A number outside the field's declared range is rejected, including one that becomes infinity.
  • A body nested past the limit is rejected without a stack trace and without the parser running to exhaustion.
  • A compressed body that decodes past the limit is rejected during decoding, measured by the bytes produced.
  • Every string and array field has a maximum length, and it is not one global number.
  • The rejection names the rule rather than echoing the value.
  • All of the above are tested, and the tests are in the build.
Download labs/contracts_lab.py. It needs nothing beyond Python 3.

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 labs/contracts_lab.py    python3 labs/contracts_lab.py

There is no python3 command on a default Windows install, so use py -3 there. Everything in this lab is real behaviour of Python's own json module on the machine you run it on. Nothing is simulated, which also means the two crash checks describe CPython: the checks compare the kind of failure rather than its message, because messages change between versions, but a different Python or a different runtime could in principle fail differently. If a check does not match on your machine, that is the lab telling you something true about your parser.

$ python3 labs/contracts_lab.py
all behaviour below is Python's json module on this machine

Part A: one body, two answers.
 1. the handler's parser reads miles as                90000
 2. a first-wins parser reads miles as                 10
 3. the two agree                                      False
 4. both parsers accepted the body                     True

Part B: values the contract never described.
 5. NaN, which is not valid JSON                       ok: nan
 6. Infinity, which is not valid JSON                  ok: inf
 7. 1e400, a number with no JSON limit                 ok: inf
 8. NaN with parse_constant refusing                   crash: ValueError
 9. a 10000-digit integer literal                      crash: ValueError
10. inf passes a schema that wants a positive number   True

Part C: shapes that cost you before any check runs.
11. 100000 levels of nesting, parsed                   crash: RecursionError
12. its depth, measured without parsing                100000
13. a depth limit of 64, applied first                 reject: too deeply nested
14. a compressed body under 64 KiB                     True
15. its decoded size over 1 MiB                        True
16. expansion ratio over 100 to 1                      True
17. a decoded-size limit of 1 MiB, applied while decoding reject: body too large

Part D: why the schema cannot do Part C's job.
18. the nested body reaches the schema at all          no, it crashed in the parser
19. the oversized body satisfies the schema            True
20. the duplicate-key body satisfies the schema        True

all lab checks passed

Checks 1 to 4 are the whole of Part A. One body, two parsers, two values, and both parsers returned successfully. There is no error to find later, because neither component did anything wrong.

Checks 8 and 9 are worth reading as a pair with the ones above them. Check 8 is a refusal you configured: parse_constant turning NaN into a rejection. Check 9 is not a refusal at all, it is the parser raising because the integer literal exceeds Python's digit limit. Both appear in a log as an exception, and only one of them is a control.

Check 11 is the one to try changing. A hundred thousand open brackets is 200 KB of input, well under any sensible body limit, and it exhausts the parser. Check 12 measures the same body's depth without parsing it, in a few lines, and check 13 refuses it. The order is the entire control.

Checks 14 to 17 are the compression case. A body that arrives under 64 KiB decodes to megabytes, and a limit that inspects the decoded object measures something you have already paid for.

Part D closes it. The nested body never reaches the schema at all, and the other two satisfy it completely. A schema was never going to be where this is caught.

Try next:

  • Change the depth in nested from 100000 to 200. Check 11 stops crashing and check 13 still refuses it, which is the difference between a limit and a cliff.
  • Pass object_pairs_hook to the handler's parse in Part A so that a repeated name raises. Both checks 1 and 3 change, and that is the fix.
  • Add a field to accepts_schema requiring miles to be below a million. Check 10 flips, and check 19 does not. Say why.
  • Take the JSON parser of another language you use and run the Part A body through it. Write down which of RFC 8259's three behaviours it implements.
8. Check your understanding

Two services parse the same request body. Why is that a security problem rather than a duplication problem?

Because a repeated name has no single meaning. RFC 8259 recommends unique names and documents three conformant behaviours when they are not: last wins, error, and all pairs kept. Two components can each behave correctly and reach different values, so a validator can approve one number while a handler acts on another. Either reject repeated names or make sure only one component parses the request.

Your schema says miles is a number greater than zero. Does infinity satisfy it?

In most implementations, yes. Infinity is not valid JSON, and Python's parser produces it anyway unless told otherwise, at which point it is a number and it is greater than zero. The fix is in the parser's configuration, not in the schema, and it needs a bounded range on the field as well.

Why can a nesting limit not live in the schema?

Because the schema runs on an object and a deeply nested body is an attack on the process of building one. The parser exhausts its stack first, so the validator that would have refused the input never executes. Depth is visible in the text, so it can be measured before parsing, which is the only place the check does any good.

You accept gzipped request bodies and limit bodies to 1 MiB. What is the limit on?

Whichever number you measured. If it is the bytes that arrived, a 64 KiB body can decode to megabytes and you have no limit on the thing that costs you. The limit has to be enforced during decompression, on the bytes produced, with the decoder stopped when it passes the threshold.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. RFC 8259 recommends unique names and records three conformant behaviours when they repeat, so two components can each be correct and disagree. Rejecting the body is the only resolution that cannot be disagreed with.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. Any rule you pick for resolving a repeated name is a rule some other parser resolves differently, and the attacker only has to send both values to find out which one takes effect. Reject the body.

blocks.html:
Quick check

A repeated name

A request body contains "miles" twice, with different values. What should the API do?

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/contracts_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant. All four change the output, and in all four the lab exits 1, because it compares every check with the result it expects.

1. The depth limit is raised to 100000

A partner's document was refused as too deep, so someone raises the limit. In check 13, change depth_of(nested) > 64 to depth_of(nested) > 100000. The check's label still says 64.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The comparison is >, and the body is exactly 100000 levels deep, so it does not exceed the new limit. It goes on to the parser.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 13 goes from reject: too deeply nested to crash: RecursionError, the same text check 11 prints. The limit still runs before the parser. It is just set past the point where the parser fails, so it refuses nothing the parser would not have crashed on anyway. Check ctr-02 in the Reference layer asks for limits that run before the parser, and a limit only counts if it is lower than what the parser can survive.
  • Check 12 prints the measured depth, 100000, and compares it with nothing. It is the same under any limit.
  • Check 18 parses the nested body with no limit in front of it. It printed no, it crashed in the parser before the edit and prints it after.

2. The handler is made to agree with the validator

The two parsers in Part A disagree, so someone makes them the same. Change the handler's parse to use the validator's rule:

handler = json.loads(body, object_pairs_hook=first_wins)
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 1 prints the handler's own reading of miles, and check 3 compares the two objects. Both depend on the line that was edited.
  • Nothing is refused. first_wins keeps the first value and returns an object, so check 4, both parsers accepted the body, still prints True.
  • Check 20 does not move. The handler now holds miles as 10, which is a positive number, so the body satisfies the schema exactly as it did at 90000.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: check 1 goes from 90000 to 10 and check 3 goes from False to True. The disagreement inside this one program is gone, and the body with miles twice is still accepted and still passes the schema. It has been resolved, not rejected, and the next component to parse the same bytes with its own default reads 90000 again, which is what check 1 printed before the edit. Check ctr-01 in the Reference layer asks for the rejection.

3. The refusing parser is sent 1e400

Check 8 parses NaN with parse_constant set to a function that raises. Keep that setting and change only the text being parsed, from "NaN" to "1e400". The check's label still says NaN.

What does check 8 print?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 8 goes from crash: ValueError to ok: inf, the same text check 7 prints with no setting at all. Measured separately by counting calls: Python's json module calls parse_constant once each for NaN, Infinity and -Infinity, and not at all for 1e400. The setting refuses three spellings, not a value. Infinity still arrives through an ordinary number that is too large, and check 10 shows it passing a schema that wants a positive number. That is why check ctr-05 in the Reference layer asks for an explicit range on every numeric field and a test with a value that becomes infinity.
  • The parser was told to refuse the constants NaN and Infinity as they are written in the text. 1e400 is written as a number, so the function that raises is never called.
  • 1e400 is valid JSON. The grammar puts no limit on the size of a number, which is what check 7's label says.
  • The parser returns a float, and this value is past the largest one a float can hold. Check 7 parses the same text and prints ok: inf.

4. The size limit is applied to the bytes that arrived

In check 17, change len(payload) > 1_048_576 to len(compressed) > 1_048_576, so the 1 MiB limit measures the body as it was received instead of as it decodes.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 14 says otherwise. The compressed body is under 64 KiB, which is far below 1 MiB, so a limit on the bytes received never fires.
  • Check 15 measures the decoded size directly and does not use the limit. It prints True before and after.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 17 goes from reject: body too large to ok. The limit is the same number and it still runs, but it now measures the one size the sender controls cheaply. Checks 14 to 16 print the same three lines as before: under 64 KiB compressed, over 1 MiB decoded, more than 100 to 1. Check ctr-03 in the Reference layer says a limit on the bytes received is not a limit on the decoded size, and this is that sentence as a one-word change.
  • Check 19 runs the schema on the decoded body, and the schema has no rule about length. The oversized body satisfied it before the edit and satisfies it after.

Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• Standard"The names within an object SHOULD be unique." When they are not, RFC 8259 section 4 records three conformant behaviours: "many implementations report the last name/value pair only. Other implementations report an error or fail to parse the object, and some implementations report all of the name/value pairs, including duplicates."
  • Standard"Numeric values that cannot be represented in the grammar below (such as Infinity and NaN) are not permitted." RFC 8259 section 6.
  • StandardRFC 8259 section 6 notes that "good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision or range than" IEEE 754 double precision provides, and that numbers implying more may indicate interoperability problems.
  • Standard"A JSON parser MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar", and an implementation "may set limits on the size of texts that it accepts", "may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting" and "may set limits on the range and precision of numbers". RFC 8259 section 9. The limits are yours to set.
  • Standard"Define and enforce a maximum size of data on all incoming parameters and payloads, such as maximum length for strings, maximum number of elements in arrays, and maximum upload file size." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
  • StandardOWASP API4:2023 lists execution timeouts, maximum allocable memory, the number of operations in a single request and the number of records per page among the limits whose absence makes an API vulnerable.
  • BaselineReject a body containing a repeated name. Do not resolve it.
  • BaselineParse each request once, or prove that every component parsing it resolves the same bytes the same way.
  • BaselineConfigure the parser to refuse NaN, Infinity and -Infinity.
  • BaselineLimit nesting depth to 64, measured from the text before parsing.
  • BaselineEnforce the decoded-size limit during decompression, stopping the decoder at the threshold, and bound the expansion ratio.
  • BaselineGive every numeric field an explicit range and every string and array field an explicit maximum length, per field rather than globally.
  • BaselineReturn one status and a stable error shape naming the rule that refused the request, never echoing the offending value.
  • OptionDo not accept compressed request bodies at all, which removes the decoded-size problem instead of bounding it.
  • OptionApply the same limits to responses you consume from other services, since a response is somebody else's body arriving at your parser.
Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

• Repeated names are rejected, not resolved Test a body with one name twice. Any silent resolution is a resolution another parser makes differently.
  • Limits run before the parser Size, decoded size and nesting depth. A schema runs on an object, and these inputs are the ones that stop an object existing.
  • Decoded size is bounded during decompression Measured on the bytes produced, with the decoder stopped at the limit. A limit on the bytes received is not this.
  • The parser refuses NaN and Infinity Neither is valid JSON. Most libraries accept them by default and offer a setting that does not.
  • Every numeric field has an explicit range The grammar bounds neither magnitude nor digit count. Test a value that becomes infinity.
  • Either one component parses the request, or they demonstrably agree Gateway and service, validator and handler, or two languages. Test the same body through each.
  • String and array fields have per-field maximum lengths A single global limit sized for the largest field is no limit for the rest.
  • Rejections name the rule and do not echo the value One status, one error shape, no attacker-controlled bytes in logs or responses.
Sources

• RFC 8259: The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format, December 2017. Sections 4, 6 and 9.
  • OWASP API Security Top 10 2023, API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption.

Teams that adopt a schema often believe they have adopted input limits, and the two lists barely overlap.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
For each endpoint that accepts a body:

  • A body with a repeated name is rejected, not resolved.
  • Two components that parse the same request agree, or only one of them parses it.
  • NaN, Infinity and -Infinity are rejected.
  • A number outside the field's declared range is rejected, including one that becomes infinity.
  • A body nested past the limit is rejected without a stack trace and without the parser running to exhaustion.
  • A compressed body that decodes past the limit is rejected during decoding, measured by the bytes produced.
  • Every string and array field has a maximum length, and it is not one global number.
  • The rejection names the rule rather than echoing the value.
  • All of the above are tested, and the tests are in the build.

sections.heading: 7. Lab
sections.html:
Download labs/contracts_lab.py. It needs nothing beyond Python 3.

Windows              macOS and Linux
py -3 labs/contracts_lab.py    python3 labs/contracts_lab.py

There is no python3 command on a default Windows install, so use py -3 there. Everything in this lab is real behaviour of Python's own json module on the machine you run it on. Nothing is simulated, which also means the two crash checks describe CPython: the checks compare the kind of failure rather than its message, because messages change between versions, but a different Python or a different runtime could in principle fail differently. If a check does not match on your machine, that is the lab telling you something true about your parser.

$ python3 labs/contracts_lab.py
all behaviour below is Python's json module on this machine

Part A: one body, two answers.
 1. the handler's parser reads miles as                90000
 2. a first-wins parser reads miles as                 10
 3. the two agree                                      False
 4. both parsers accepted the body                     True

Part B: values the contract never described.
 5. NaN, which is not valid JSON                       ok: nan
 6. Infinity, which is not valid JSON                  ok: inf
 7. 1e400, a number with no JSON limit                 ok: inf
 8. NaN with parse_constant refusing                   crash: ValueError
 9. a 10000-digit integer literal                      crash: ValueError
10. inf passes a schema that wants a positive number   True

Part C: shapes that cost you before any check runs.
11. 100000 levels of nesting, parsed                   crash: RecursionError
12. its depth, measured without parsing                100000
13. a depth limit of 64, applied first                 reject: too deeply nested
14. a compressed body under 64 KiB                     True
15. its decoded size over 1 MiB                        True
16. expansion ratio over 100 to 1                      True
17. a decoded-size limit of 1 MiB, applied while decoding reject: body too large

Part D: why the schema cannot do Part C's job.
18. the nested body reaches the schema at all          no, it crashed in the parser
19. the oversized body satisfies the schema            True
20. the duplicate-key body satisfies the schema        True

all lab checks passed

Checks 1 to 4 are the whole of Part A. One body, two parsers, two values, and both parsers returned successfully. There is no error to find later, because neither component did anything wrong.

Checks 8 and 9 are worth reading as a pair with the ones above them. Check 8 is a refusal you configured: parse_constant turning NaN into a rejection. Check 9 is not a refusal at all, it is the parser raising because the integer literal exceeds Python's digit limit. Both appear in a log as an exception, and only one of them is a control.

Check 11 is the one to try changing. A hundred thousand open brackets is 200 KB of input, well under any sensible body limit, and it exhausts the parser. Check 12 measures the same body's depth without parsing it, in a few lines, and check 13 refuses it. The order is the entire control.

Checks 14 to 17 are the compression case. A body that arrives under 64 KiB decodes to megabytes, and a limit that inspects the decoded object measures something you have already paid for.

Part D closes it. The nested body never reaches the schema at all, and the other two satisfy it completely. A schema was never going to be where this is caught.

Try next:

  • Change the depth in nested from 100000 to 200. Check 11 stops crashing and check 13 still refuses it, which is the difference between a limit and a cliff.
  • Pass object_pairs_hook to the handler's parse in Part A so that a repeated name raises. Both checks 1 and 3 change, and that is the fix.
  • Add a field to accepts_schema requiring miles to be below a million. Check 10 flips, and check 19 does not. Say why.
  • Take the JSON parser of another language you use and run the Part A body through it. Write down which of RFC 8259's three behaviours it implements.

sections.heading: 8. Check your understanding
sections.html:
Two services parse the same request body. Why is that a security problem rather than a duplication problem?

Because a repeated name has no single meaning. RFC 8259 recommends unique names and documents three conformant behaviours when they are not: last wins, error, and all pairs kept. Two components can each behave correctly and reach different values, so a validator can approve one number while a handler acts on another. Either reject repeated names or make sure only one component parses the request.

Your schema says miles is a number greater than zero. Does infinity satisfy it?

In most implementations, yes. Infinity is not valid JSON, and Python's parser produces it anyway unless told otherwise, at which point it is a number and it is greater than zero. The fix is in the parser's configuration, not in the schema, and it needs a bounded range on the field as well.

Why can a nesting limit not live in the schema?

Because the schema runs on an object and a deeply nested body is an attack on the process of building one. The parser exhausts its stack first, so the validator that would have refused the input never executes. Depth is visible in the text, so it can be measured before parsing, which is the only place the check does any good.

You accept gzipped request bodies and limit bodies to 1 MiB. What is the limit on?

Whichever number you measured. If it is the bytes that arrived, a 64 KiB body can decode to megabytes and you have no limit on the thing that costs you. The limit has to be enforced during decompression, on the bytes produced, with the decoder stopped when it passes the threshold.

Quick check

sections.heading: A repeated name
sections.html:
A request body contains "miles" twice, with different values. What should the API do?

Exercises

sections.heading: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.heading_text: Change one thing and predict the output
sections.html:
Each exercise edits one place in labs/contracts_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant. All four change the output, and in all four the lab exits 1, because it compares every check with the result it expects.

1. The depth limit is raised to 100000

A partner's document was refused as too deep, so someone raises the limit. In check 13, change depth_of(nested) > 64 to depth_of(nested) > 100000. The check's label still says 64.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • The comparison is >, and the body is exactly 100000 levels deep, so it does not exceed the new limit. It goes on to the parser.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 13 goes from reject: too deeply nested to crash: RecursionError, the same text check 11 prints. The limit still runs before the parser. It is just set past the point where the parser fails, so it refuses nothing the parser would not have crashed on anyway. Check ctr-02 in the Reference layer asks for limits that run before the parser, and a limit only counts if it is lower than what the parser can survive.
  • Check 12 prints the measured depth, 100000, and compares it with nothing. It is the same under any limit.
  • Check 18 parses the nested body with no limit in front of it. It printed no, it crashed in the parser before the edit and prints it after.

2. The handler is made to agree with the validator

The two parsers in Part A disagree, so someone makes them the same. Change the handler's parse to use the validator's rule:

handler = json.loads(body, object_pairs_hook=first_wins)
What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 1 prints the handler's own reading of miles, and check 3 compares the two objects. Both depend on the line that was edited.
  • Nothing is refused. first_wins keeps the first value and returns an object, so check 4, both parsers accepted the body, still prints True.
  • Check 20 does not move. The handler now holds miles as 10, which is a positive number, so the body satisfies the schema exactly as it did at 90000.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: check 1 goes from 90000 to 10 and check 3 goes from False to True. The disagreement inside this one program is gone, and the body with miles twice is still accepted and still passes the schema. It has been resolved, not rejected, and the next component to parse the same bytes with its own default reads 90000 again, which is what check 1 printed before the edit. Check ctr-01 in the Reference layer asks for the rejection.

3. The refusing parser is sent 1e400

Check 8 parses NaN with parse_constant set to a function that raises. Keep that setting and change only the text being parsed, from "NaN" to "1e400". The check's label still says NaN.

What does check 8 print?

Every option, and why
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 8 goes from crash: ValueError to ok: inf, the same text check 7 prints with no setting at all. Measured separately by counting calls: Python's json module calls parse_constant once each for NaN, Infinity and -Infinity, and not at all for 1e400. The setting refuses three spellings, not a value. Infinity still arrives through an ordinary number that is too large, and check 10 shows it passing a schema that wants a positive number. That is why check ctr-05 in the Reference layer asks for an explicit range on every numeric field and a test with a value that becomes infinity.
  • The parser was told to refuse the constants NaN and Infinity as they are written in the text. 1e400 is written as a number, so the function that raises is never called.
  • 1e400 is valid JSON. The grammar puts no limit on the size of a number, which is what check 7's label says.
  • The parser returns a float, and this value is past the largest one a float can hold. Check 7 parses the same text and prints ok: inf.

4. The size limit is applied to the bytes that arrived

In check 17, change len(payload) > 1_048_576 to len(compressed) > 1_048_576, so the 1 MiB limit measures the body as it was received instead of as it decodes.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 14 says otherwise. The compressed body is under 64 KiB, which is far below 1 MiB, so a limit on the bytes received never fires.
  • Check 15 measures the decoded size directly and does not use the limit. It prints True before and after.
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 17 goes from reject: body too large to ok. The limit is the same number and it still runs, but it now measures the one size the sender controls cheaply. Checks 14 to 16 print the same three lines as before: under 64 KiB compressed, over 1 MiB decoded, more than 100 to 1. Check ctr-03 in the Reference layer says a limit on the bytes received is not a limit on the decoded size, and this is that sentence as a one-word change.
  • Check 19 runs the schema on the decoded body, and the schema has no rule about length. The oversized body satisfied it before the edit and satisfies it after.

Course progress: return to the course dashboard to see your published-module progress.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.html:
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

  • Standard"The names within an object SHOULD be unique." When they are not, RFC 8259 section 4 records three conformant behaviours: "many implementations report the last name/value pair only. Other implementations report an error or fail to parse the object, and some implementations report all of the name/value pairs, including duplicates."
  • Standard"Numeric values that cannot be represented in the grammar below (such as Infinity and NaN) are not permitted." RFC 8259 section 6.
  • StandardRFC 8259 section 6 notes that "good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision or range than" IEEE 754 double precision provides, and that numbers implying more may indicate interoperability problems.
  • Standard"A JSON parser MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar", and an implementation "may set limits on the size of texts that it accepts", "may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting" and "may set limits on the range and precision of numbers". RFC 8259 section 9. The limits are yours to set.
  • Standard"Define and enforce a maximum size of data on all incoming parameters and payloads, such as maximum length for strings, maximum number of elements in arrays, and maximum upload file size." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
  • StandardOWASP API4:2023 lists execution timeouts, maximum allocable memory, the number of operations in a single request and the number of records per page among the limits whose absence makes an API vulnerable.
  • BaselineReject a body containing a repeated name. Do not resolve it.
  • BaselineParse each request once, or prove that every component parsing it resolves the same bytes the same way.
  • BaselineConfigure the parser to refuse NaN, Infinity and -Infinity.
  • BaselineLimit nesting depth to 64, measured from the text before parsing.
  • BaselineEnforce the decoded-size limit during decompression, stopping the decoder at the threshold, and bound the expansion ratio.
  • BaselineGive every numeric field an explicit range and every string and array field an explicit maximum length, per field rather than globally.
  • BaselineReturn one status and a stable error shape naming the rule that refused the request, never echoing the offending value.
  • OptionDo not accept compressed request bodies at all, which removes the decoded-size problem instead of bounding it.
  • OptionApply the same limits to responses you consume from other services, since a response is somebody else's body arriving at your parser.

sections.heading: Review checklist items
sections.html:
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • Repeated names are rejected, not resolved Test a body with one name twice. Any silent resolution is a resolution another parser makes differently.
  • Limits run before the parser Size, decoded size and nesting depth. A schema runs on an object, and these inputs are the ones that stop an object existing.
  • Decoded size is bounded during decompression Measured on the bytes produced, with the decoder stopped at the limit. A limit on the bytes received is not this.
  • The parser refuses NaN and Infinity Neither is valid JSON. Most libraries accept them by default and offer a setting that does not.
  • Every numeric field has an explicit range The grammar bounds neither magnitude nor digit count. Test a value that becomes infinity.
  • Either one component parses the request, or they demonstrably agree Gateway and service, validator and handler, or two languages. Test the same body through each.
  • String and array fields have per-field maximum lengths A single global limit sized for the largest field is no limit for the rest.
  • Rejections name the rule and do not echo the value One status, one error shape, no attacker-controlled bytes in logs or responses.

Your schema says miles is a number greater than zero. Does infinity satisfy it?

In most implementations, yes. Infinity is not valid JSON, and Python's parser produces it anyway unless told otherwise, at which point it is a number and it is greater than zero. The fix is in the parser's configuration, not in the schema, and it needs a bounded range on the field as well.

quiz.summary: Why can a nesting limit not live in the schema?
quiz.html:
Why can a nesting limit not live in the schema?

Because the schema runs on an object and a deeply nested body is an attack on the process of building one. The parser exhausts its stack first, so the validator that would have refused the input never executes. Depth is visible in the text, so it can be measured before parsing, which is the only place the check does any good.

quiz.summary: You accept gzipped request bodies and limit bodies to 1 MiB. What is the limit on?
quiz.html:
You accept gzipped request bodies and limit bodies to 1 MiB. What is the limit on?

Whichever number you measured. If it is the bytes that arrived, a 64 KiB body can decode to megabytes and you have no limit on the thing that costs you. The limit has to be enforced during decompression, on the bytes produced, with the decoder stopped when it passes the threshold.

exercises.heading: 1. The depth limit is raised to 100000
exercises.heading_text: 1. The depth limit is raised to 100000
exercises.legend: What does the run print differently?

options.label: Nothing. A body 100000 levels deep is still refused by a limit of 100000.
Check 12 changes, because the depth is measured against the new limit.

answers.html: The comparison is >, and the body is exactly 100000 levels deep, so it does not exceed the new limit. It goes on to the parser.

Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 13 goes from reject: too deeply nested to crash: RecursionError, the same text check 11 prints. The limit still runs before the parser. It is just set past the point where the parser fails, so it refuses nothing the parser would not have crashed on anyway. Check ctr-02 in the Reference layer asks for limits that run before the parser, and a limit only counts if it is lower than what the parser can survive.
Check 12 prints the measured depth, 100000, and compares it with nothing. It is the same under any limit.
Check 18 parses the nested body with no limit in front of it. It printed no, it crashed in the parser before the edit and prints it after.

exercises.heading: 2. The handler is made to agree with the validator
exercises.heading_text: 2. The handler is made to agree with the validator
exercises.legend: What does the run print differently?

options.label: Nothing. The checks compare the validator's reading, not the handler's.
Check 3 becomes True and check 4 becomes False, because the repeated name is now refused.
Check 1 becomes 10 and check 3 becomes True. Checks 4 and 20 still print True.

answers.html: Check 1 prints the handler's own reading of miles, and check 3 compares the two objects. Both depend on the line that was edited.
Nothing is refused. first_wins keeps the first value and returns an object, so check 4, both parsers accepted the body, still prints True.
Check 20 does not move. The handler now holds miles as 10, which is a positive number, so the body satisfies the schema exactly as it did at 90000.

Correct. Exit 1, two failures: check 1 goes from 90000 to 10 and check 3 goes from False to True. The disagreement inside this one program is gone, and the body with miles twice is still accepted and still passes the schema. It has been resolved, not rejected, and the next component to parse the same bytes with its own default reads 90000 again, which is what check 1 printed before the edit. Check ctr-01 in the Reference layer asks for the rejection.

exercises.heading: 3. The refusing parser is sent 1e400

options.label: crash: ValueError, as before. The parser was told to refuse infinity.
reject: JSONDecodeError, because a number that large is not valid JSON.

answers.html: Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 8 goes from crash: ValueError to ok: inf, the same text check 7 prints with no setting at all. Measured separately by counting calls: Python's json module calls parse_constant once each for NaN, Infinity and -Infinity, and not at all for 1e400. The setting refuses three spellings, not a value. Infinity still arrives through an ordinary number that is too large, and check 10 shows it passing a schema that wants a positive number. That is why check ctr-05 in the Reference layer asks for an explicit range on every numeric field and a test with a value that becomes infinity.
The parser was told to refuse the constants NaN and Infinity as they are written in the text. 1e400 is written as a number, so the function that raises is never called.
1e400 is valid JSON. The grammar puts no limit on the size of a number, which is what check 7's label says.
The parser returns a float, and this value is past the largest one a float can hold. Check 7 parses the same text and prints ok: inf.

exercises.heading: 4. The size limit is applied to the bytes that arrived
exercises.heading_text: 4. The size limit is applied to the bytes that arrived
exercises.legend: What does the run print differently?

options.label: Nothing. The body is over 1 MiB whichever way it is measured.
Check 17 becomes ok and check 19 becomes False.

answers.html: Check 14 says otherwise. The compressed body is under 64 KiB, which is far below 1 MiB, so a limit on the bytes received never fires.
Check 15 measures the decoded size directly and does not use the limit. It prints True before and after.

Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 17 goes from reject: body too large to ok. The limit is the same number and it still runs, but it now measures the one size the sender controls cheaply. Checks 14 to 16 print the same three lines as before: under 64 KiB compressed, over 1 MiB decoded, more than 100 to 1. Check ctr-03 in the Reference layer says a limit on the bytes received is not a limit on the decoded size, and this is that sentence as a one-word change.
Check 19 runs the schema on the decoded body, and the schema has no rule about length. The oversized body satisfied it before the edit and satisfies it after.
